network.overall_strategy: Construct ten experimentally distinguishable catalyst/reagent-specific pathways spanning four mechanistic families: ammonia reductive amination, hydroxylamine-mediated reductive amination, pyridoxamine transamination, and malonate–glyoxylate coupling/decarboxylation. These are ten operational pathways, not ten independent carbon-skeleton mechanisms. The network contains 18 molecule nodes and 14 reaction nodes, including competing oxaloacetate decay and carbonyl reduction. It is complete at the declared precursor boundary: oxaloacetate, glyoxylate, malonate, pyridoxamine, nitrogen sources, and reductants are supplied inventories; their continuous production from CO2 is not claimed. The substrate-specific Strecker and fumaronitrile reconstructions are excluded because the supplied evidence does not establish their selective environmental hydrolysis. Each pathway occupies a separate anoxic, UV-shielded aqueous compartment; shared molecule IDs indicate chemical identity, not one-pot compatibility or physical pooling. All transformations are assigned to Biochemical because the supported assembly chemistry occurs in cool aqueous pools or mineral interfaces, rather than hot vent interiors. Neutral parent formulas represent precursor acid–base pools; the target explicitly represents net-negative, stereochemically unspecified aspartate. H+ denotes buffer-mediated proton accounting, not an acidic bulk solution. Experimental yields are distinguished from proposed operating conditions. No quantitative end-to-end environmental yield, selective cleanup, or sustained precursor supply is assumed.

reactions.name: Oxaloacetate reductive amination by partially electroreduced FeS–Fe0
agents: Partially electroreduced FeS containing Fe0 nanodomains; the consumed Fe0 inventory is explicitly represented by mol_004

conditions.pressure: Approximately 1 bar under an inert, anoxic headspace
conditions.catalyst: Electroreduced FeS host promoting adsorption and electron transfer; Fe0 is a consumable reductant
conditions.other: Reported benchmark: 5 mM oxaloacetate, 0.5 M ammonia inventory, pH 9.6, 48 h. The experimental material was preconditioned at -0.7 V versus SHE for seven days; this preparation is an external material boundary, not an assumed spontaneous activation step. Use freshly prepared oxaloacetate and an opaque reactor. Quantify active Fe0 rather than equating total FeS mass with reducing capacity. Buffer exchange supplies the formal proton input. Actual Fe(II) partitioning among dissolved complexes and secondary solids is not resolved by the molecular bookkeeping.

reactions.mechanism: Ammonia forms an oxaloacetate-derived imine or iminium species; electron transfer from embedded Fe0 reduces the C=N group to the amino-acid oxidation state. Fe0 oxidation supplies the required reducing equivalents.
reactions.reasoning: Kitadai et al. (2019) reported 64% Asp from supplied oxaloacetate under these mild assay conditions. Ordinary FeS is not an equivalent catalyst, and the electroreduced surface architecture matters. The yield is an isolated-substrate benchmark, not an environmental or CO2-to-Asp yield. Concentrating ammonia to 0.5 M, maintaining fresh oxaloacetate, and generating the active material naturally remain unresolved. Competing oxaloacetate decay is explicitly represented by rxn_013.

reactions.name: Oxaloacetate reductive amination by native Fe0 without an FeS host
agents: Reactive Fe0 surface, with Fe0 consumed as the electron donor

conditions.pressure: Approximately 1 bar under an inert, anoxic headspace
conditions.catalyst: Fe0 surface; not a nonconsumable catalyst
conditions.other: Use the matched oxaloacetate/ammonia comparison regime: 5 mM oxaloacetate, 0.5 M ammonia inventory, pH 9.6, and observations through 48 h. Introduce oxaloacetate only after preparing the anoxic metal suspension. Accessible Fe0 must exceed the electron-balance minimum; an optimal loading or natural-grain activity is not specified by the supplied summary. Record passivation and early pyruvate formation. Do not combine this compartment with pyridoxamine/Cu2+ or Al3+ branches.

reactions.mechanism: Surface-assisted imine formation and reduction consume metallic iron, producing aspartate and an Fe(II) oxidation inventory without requiring an FeS host.
reactions.reasoning: Kitadai et al. (2019) found that Fe0 alone also produces Asp, but with greater oxaloacetate decarboxylation and pyruvate/alanine formation than the FeS–Fe0 material. This is an experimentally supported alternative to P1, not an assumed equivalent of its 64% yield. Native-metal availability, surface condition, and competing decay determine its geochemical performance.

reactions.name: Hydrogen-driven oxaloacetate reductive amination over supported nickel
agents: Ni on SiO2–Al2O3, 10 mol% Ni relative to oxaloacetate

conditions.other: Reported standard regime: 30 mM ketoacid, five equivalents NH4HCO3, pH 8, and 72 h. The nitrogen node represents the ammonia/ammonium equilibrium pool. Establish anoxia and H2 availability before adding fresh oxaloacetate. Keep sulfide and cyanide out of this compartment because they can alter or poison the metal surface. Maintain liquid–gas contact; do not infer dissolved H2 solely from nominal headspace pressure. Track rxn_013 and rxn_014 concurrently.

reactions.mechanism: Nickel activates H2 and hydrogenates the imine formed from oxaloacetate and ammonia. Direct carbonyl hydrogenation competes with imine reduction.
reactions.reasoning: Kaur et al. (2024) demonstrated Asp formation with H2 and supported Ni. Their 6–84% range across Ni/meteorite experiments refers to combined amino-plus-hydroxy products across a substrate panel, not an Asp-specific yield. The reported low-ammonia quantitative result was for alanine and is not transferred to Asp. Supported Ni is a controlled experimental catalyst; equivalent activity of natural Ni grains is not assumed.

reactions.name: Hydrogen-driven oxaloacetate reductive amination over meteoritic Fe–Ni metal
agents: Ground iron-meteorite metal containing approximately 11-18 mol% Ni

conditions.other: Use the reported standard aqueous comparison framework: 30 mM oxaloacetate, five equivalents NH4HCO3, pH 8, and 72 h. Use ground rather than intact meteorite material. Meteorite mass, exposed area, and particle-size distribution are essential experimental variables but are not numerically specified in the supplied summary; no equivalent natural-grain rate is assigned. Keep the reactor anoxic, UV-shielded, and separate from sulfide-rich fluids. Metal corrosion may change the catalyst during operation.

reactions.mechanism: Ni-bearing sites in the natural metal mixture activate H2 and reduce an oxaloacetate–ammonia imine, with carbonyl reduction and oxaloacetate decay competing.
reactions.reasoning: Kaur et al. (2024) demonstrated amino-acid production, including Asp, using several ground iron meteorites. This supports natural heterogeneous-metal catalysis without requiring that Asp historically formed inside meteorites. It does not establish performance for unground grains, dilute seawater, or arbitrary Fe–Ni compositions. The missing surface/loading specification is retained as an explicit operational uncertainty rather than replaced with an invented optimum.

reactions.name: Hydrogen-driven oxaloacetate reductive amination over palladium
agents: Pd/C, 1 mol% Pd relative to oxaloacetate

conditions.other: Reported standard regime: 30 mM ketoacid, five equivalents NH4HCO3, pH 8, and 72 h. Use fresh oxaloacetate in a separately maintained, anoxic and UV-shielded compartment. Exclude cyanide and uncontrolled sulfide exposure. This is a catalyst-performance reference; no abundant natural Pd/C deposit or environmental catalyst concentration is assumed.

reactions.mechanism: Pd dissociates H2 and reduces the oxaloacetate-derived imine; competing keto-group reduction can form malate.
reactions.reasoning: Kaur et al. (2024) demonstrated Pd-mediated reductive amination and approximately 5% Asp in their more complex OAA–glyoxylate network. Their 52–88% combined amino/hydroxy yield range across isolated substrates is not an Asp-specific yield. Pd is retained as an experimentally supported alternative, while its rarity and the artificial carbon support weaken its environmental case relative to some Fe/Ni systems.

reactions.name: Hydroxylamine-mediated conversion of oxaloacetate to aspartate with Fe0
agents: Reactive Fe0 surface, consumed during oxime reduction

conditions.temperature: 298-343 K proposed trapping window; 343 K is the reported upstream carbon-network temperature
conditions.pressure: Approximately 1 bar under an inert, anoxic headspace
conditions.other: Operate as a separate trapping stage, not simultaneously with Fe2+-promoted carbon-skeleton construction. Proposed screening inventory: 5 mM fresh oxaloacetate, 10 mM hydroxylamine, and at least 20 mM accessible Fe0, initially near neutral pH. These concentrations are design choices, not a reproduced Muchowska protocol. Sample early for Asp and pyruvate and cool promptly after useful conversion. The net chemistry requires more reducing equivalents than ammonia reductive amination because both the N–O and C=N functionalities must be reduced.

reactions.mechanism: Oxaloacetate condenses with hydroxylamine to form an oxime-like intermediate. Fe0 then reduces the nitrogen–oxygen and carbon–nitrogen unsaturation to furnish aspartate. The reaction node represents the net transformation rather than asserting isolation of the oxime.
reactions.reasoning: Muchowska, Varma and Moran (2019) detected Asp after adding hydroxylamine and Fe0 to their Fe2+-driven carbon network and supported the interpretation with ketoacid experiments. The transformation is experimentally supported, but the proposed operating window and concentrations here require validation and inherit no reported Asp yield. Hydroxylamine sourcing remains uncertain. Kaur et al. (2024) identify interference between this amination system and Fe2+-driven carbon chemistry, motivating the explicit staging.

reactions.name: Cu2+-promoted pyridoxamine transamination of oxaloacetate
agents: Cu2+, 1 mM in the representative metal-ion screen

conditions.pressure: Approximately 1 bar in a sealed, anoxic aqueous compartment
conditions.catalyst: Cu2+ coordinated by pyridoxamine and reaction intermediates
conditions.other: Representative reported screen: 10 mM oxaloacetate, 10 mM pyridoxamine, 50 mM ammonium bicarbonate, pH 7.8, and 1 mM metal ion; evaluate product formation within 1 h. Introduce oxaloacetate immediately before starting the reaction. Keep this compartment separate from Fe0, H2S-rich fluids, and cyanide. Pyridoxamine is a stoichiometric amino donor here; no cofactor-regeneration cycle is assumed.

reactions.mechanism: Metal-assisted Schiff-base chemistry transfers the amino group of pyridoxamine to oxaloacetate, producing aspartate while oxidizing the donor toward pyridoxal.
reactions.reasoning: Harrison et al. (2023) reported approximately 5% Asp within one hour with Cu2+-promoted pyridoxamine chemistry, demonstrating competition with oxaloacetate decay. This is not evidence that pyridoxamine is readily available prebiotically. Cu2+ availability in an anoxic, reduced-iron-rich world also requires a locally suitable ligand and redox setting; contact with sulfide or metallic iron cannot be assumed compatible.

reactions.name: Ni2+-promoted pyridoxamine transamination of oxaloacetate
agents: Dissolved Ni2+, 1 mM in the representative metal-ion screen

conditions.pressure: Approximately 1 bar in a sealed, anoxic aqueous compartment
conditions.catalyst: Ni2+ coordinated by pyridoxamine and ketoacid-derived ligands
conditions.other: Representative reported comparison: 10 mM oxaloacetate, 10 mM pyridoxamine, 50 mM ammonium bicarbonate, pH 7.8, and 1 mM Ni2+; assess on the one-hour timescale. Do not substitute metallic Ni or apply the 5 bar H2 protocol: this is soluble-ion transamination, not hydrogenation. Avoid sulfide-rich fluid mixing that would remove dissolved Ni2+. Keep the donor and product inventories separate from the Cu2+ and Al3+ experiments.

reactions.mechanism: Ni2+ promotes ligand-organized Schiff-base formation and amino-group transfer from pyridoxamine to oxaloacetate.
reactions.reasoning: Harrison et al. (2023) observed measurable Asp with Ni2+ in their metal-ion screen, although Cu2+ was substantially more effective. No 5% yield is assigned to the Ni2+ branch. This is a distinct experimentally tested catalyst pathway, not an independent carbon-skeleton synthesis. Nickel availability may be more plausible than palladium availability, but dissolved Ni2+ and metallic hydrogenation-active Ni are chemically different inventories.

reactions.name: Al3+-promoted pyridoxamine transamination of oxaloacetate
agents: Al3+, 1 mM nominal loading in the representative metal-ion screen

conditions.pressure: Approximately 1 bar in a sealed, anoxic aqueous compartment
conditions.other: Representative reported comparison: 10 mM oxaloacetate, 10 mM pyridoxamine, 50 mM ammonium bicarbonate, pH 7.8, and 1 mM nominal Al3+; evaluate on the one-hour timescale. Monitor precipitation because nominal added aluminum is not equivalent to dissolved active aluminum. Avoid phosphate-rich media and do not presume that ordinary aluminosilicate minerals supply 1 mM catalytically available Al at this pH. Keep this as a separate compartment.

reactions.mechanism: Lewis-acid coordination promotes pyridoxamine–oxaloacetate Schiff-base chemistry and transamination without requiring molecular hydrogen or a metal reductant.
reactions.reasoning: Harrison et al. (2023) reported measurable Asp with Al3+, weaker than with Cu2+. Its inclusion is based on an experimentally tested reaction rather than assumed mineral abundance. Near-neutral aluminum solubility, pyridoxamine supply, and precipitation are substantial geochemical limitations. Kaur et al. (2024) also discuss incompatibility between Al3+-mediated transamination and some phosphate-mediated carbon chemistry; no such one-pot coupling is asserted here.

reactions.name: Cold formation of alpha-hydroxyglycine from glyoxylate and ammonia

conditions.other: Use glyoxylic acid with concentrated ammonium acetate under cold, anoxic, UV-shielded conditions. Ammonium acetate supplies the ammonia/ammonium reservoir and buffering; acetate is not a carbon donor in this net transformation. The supplied research does not state the exact preparative molarity or isolation duration, so these must not be inferred from the reported yield. The experimentally prepared adduct is isolated cold before the concentrated coupling stage; an efficient natural isolation mechanism remains unestablished.

reactions.mechanism: Nucleophilic addition of ammonia to the glyoxylate carbonyl forms the carbinolamine alpha-hydroxyglycine without net elimination of water.
reactions.reasoning: Springsteen et al. (2018) isolated alpha-hydroxyglycine in greater than 95% yield using concentrated ammonium acetate at 0 degrees C. This supports the molecular intermediate and transformation, not its quantitative accumulation in a dilute environmental pool. Cold operation is represented directly rather than changing the experiment to a warm surface temperature. Availability of concentrated reduced nitrogen and retention of the reversible adduct remain upstream constraints.

reactions.name: Malonate coupling with alpha-hydroxyglycine to beta-carboxyaspartate

conditions.other: Reported regime: 480 mM malonic acid, two equivalents alpha-hydroxyglycine, 1 M bicarbonate, initial pH 7.2, and five days. Prepare the concentrated malonate/bicarbonate inventory before introducing the labile nitrogenous adduct. Keep the reaction wet, anoxic, and UV-shielded; repeated irradiation or drying during the five-day reaction is not part of the demonstrated protocol. No transition-metal catalyst is required. Do not import Fe0, Cu2+, Ni catalysts, or other branch residues.

reactions.mechanism: Malonate-derived carbon nucleophilicity couples with the glyoxylate-derived carbinolamine/iminium system, forming the C–C bond of beta-carboxyaspartate with net loss of water.
reactions.reasoning: Springsteen et al. (2018) demonstrated this condensation as the first step of a two-step, 50%-overall-yield malonate-to-Asp sequence. The five-day residence time is a key kinetic bottleneck. The unusually high malonate, adduct, and bicarbonate concentrations are experimentally important and cannot be replaced by dilute-ocean concentrations while retaining the reported performance. Evaporative concentration is a possible upstream operation, not a demonstrated complete supply chain.

reactions.name: Mg2+-promoted beta-carboxyaspartate decarboxylation
agents: Mg2+ supplied as MgCl2, approximately one equivalent in the reported sequence

conditions.catalyst: Mg2+ Lewis-acid promoter; the reported loading is stoichiometric rather than a demonstrated low-loading catalyst
conditions.other: After the five-day condensation, add approximately one equivalent MgCl2 and heat for five hours at 333 K. This is a staged change in the same malonate-route inventory, not mixing with another pathway. Retain the bicarbonate-based medium and avoid introducing phosphate that could sequester Mg2+. Cool after the reaction rather than storing Asp in a hotter hydrothermal zone. Formal H+ release reflects the explicitly anionic target representation.

reactions.mechanism: Mg2+ coordination facilitates loss of one malonate-derived carboxyl group as CO2; proton redistribution furnishes aspartate.
reactions.reasoning: Springsteen et al. (2018) reported 50% overall Asp yield across the condensation and Mg2+-promoted decarboxylation sequence. That number is not an isolated yield for this reaction and is not multiplied by unrelated laboratory yields to claim environmental throughput. The branch bypasses oxaloacetate instability but still requires concentrated malonate and alpha-hydroxyglycine. Cooler post-reaction storage is consistent with the Asp-destruction concerns documented by Cox and Seward (2007) and Estrada et al. (2017).

reactions.name: Competing oxaloacetate decarboxylation to pyruvate

conditions.temperature: 295-343 K, matching the relevant productive compartment
conditions.pressure: Approximately 1 bar or 5 bar H2, according to the competing pathway
conditions.other: Evaluate under each pathway's actual pH, temperature, buffer, and metal exposure rather than assigning one universal half-life. Spontaneous decay requires no added catalyst; metal coordination can modify its rate. Use fresh oxaloacetate, collect early time points, and compare pyruvate production directly with Asp production. This node is a competing sink, not a productive Asp pathway.

reactions.mechanism: The beta-keto-acid arrangement of oxaloacetate undergoes decarboxylation, producing pyruvate and CO2.
reactions.reasoning: Kitadai et al. (2019), Harrison et al. (2023), and Kaur et al. (2024) identify oxaloacetate instability as a central constraint on Asp synthesis. A nominally high terminal conversion cannot be interpreted independently of this competing flux. Reported hour-scale instability does not establish a transferable rate constant for every metal, pH, and temperature used in the network.

reactions.name: Competing nickel-catalyzed reduction of oxaloacetate to malate
agents: Ni on SiO2–Al2O3, using the same catalyst inventory as rxn_003

conditions.other: Competes in the rxn_003 compartment: 30 mM initial oxaloacetate, five equivalents NH4HCO3, pH 8, and observations through 72 h. Ammonia is present but is not consumed by this branch. Record malate separately from Asp; combined amino-plus-hydroxy product yield is not an amino-acid yield. Lower pH or insufficient reactive ammonia can shift selectivity toward carbonyl reduction.

reactions.mechanism: Surface hydrogenation reduces the keto group directly to a hydroxyl group instead of reducing an ammonia-derived imine.
reactions.reasoning: Kaur et al. (2024) describe competing amino-acid and hydroxy-acid formation during metal/H2 reduction of ketoacids and pH-dependent product selectivity. Including malate prevents total reduced-product yield from being misreported as Asp yield. This explicitly represents the Ni side branch; it does not assume identical rates or selectivity for Pd and meteoritic catalysts.

pathways.name: Electroreduced FeS–Fe0 ammonia pathway
pathways.description: Direct conversion of supplied oxaloacetate with ammonia using an activated FeS–Fe0 material. The 64% experimental benchmark is conditional on the reported substrate, nitrogen, and material preparation.

pathways.name: Native Fe0 ammonia pathway
pathways.description: Direct ammonia reductive amination without an FeS host. Experimentally supported but less selective because oxaloacetate decay competes strongly.

pathways.name: Supported-Ni/H2 ammonia pathway
pathways.description: Hydrogen-driven reductive amination over supported Ni. Pyruvate and malate sinks must be quantified alongside Asp.

pathways.name: Meteoritic Fe–Ni/H2 ammonia pathway
pathways.description: Hydrogen-driven reductive amination using a tested natural heterogeneous metal source. Ground-material performance is not assigned to intact environmental grains.

pathways.name: Pd/H2 ammonia pathway
pathways.description: An experimentally supported hydrogenation comparator with favorable laboratory performance but restricted geochemical catalyst availability.

pathways.name: Hydroxylamine/Fe0 trapping pathway
pathways.description: Oxime-mediated conversion of supplied oxaloacetate, operated separately from Fe2+-driven precursor construction. Hydroxylamine sourcing and the proposed operating window remain unresolved.

pathways.name: Cu2+/pyridoxamine transamination pathway
pathways.description: Rapid metal-assisted amino-group transfer from supplied pyridoxamine. Pyridoxamine is consumed, and its prebiotic synthesis and regeneration are outside the demonstrated boundary.

pathways.name: Ni2+/pyridoxamine transamination pathway
pathways.description: The experimentally tested soluble-nickel alternative to Cu2+-promoted transamination, distinct from metallic-Ni/H2 chemistry and not assigned the Cu2+ yield.

pathways.name: Al3+/pyridoxamine transamination pathway
pathways.description: An experimentally tested Lewis-acid transamination alternative. Aluminum solubility, ligand stabilization, and phosphate incompatibility limit environmental extrapolation.

pathways.name: Glyoxylate–malonate assembly and decarboxylation pathway
pathways.description: Cold glyoxylate amination produces alpha-hydroxyglycine, which couples with concentrated malonate before Mg2+-promoted decarboxylation to Asp. This staged branch constructs the target skeleton without oxaloacetate or an external reductant, but it does not establish environmental feedstock concentration or adduct isolation.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Strong direct support comes from Kitadai et al. (2019): electroreduced FeS–Fe0 produced 64% Asp from supplied oxaloacetate. The balanced equation correctly represents Fe0 as a consumed reductant. However, the generic cool aqueous compartment does not establish the required surface state, ammonia concentration, pH or reaction time. The reported yield belongs to the experimental conditions, not automatically to this environmental implementation.
suggestions: Attach the experimental reference conditions: 5 mM oxaloacetate, 0.5 M ammonia, pH 9.6, 23–25 °C and 48 hours; distinguish any proposed departures.
Specify the inventory and preservation of the active FeS–Fe0 composite, including whether it is supplied preactivated or generated locally.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Kitadai et al. (2019) support Asp formation with Fe0 without an FeS host. This is a valid operational alternative, although oxaloacetate decarboxylation and subsequent alanine formation reduce selectivity. Including rxn_013 appropriately represents the initial competing carbon-loss step. Experimental Fe0 reactivity does not establish identical behavior for unspecified native grains.
suggestions: Specify Fe0 grain size, surface oxidation or passivation, loading, ammonia concentration, pH and residence time.
Use native-metal measurements to compare Asp formation against oxaloacetate decay rather than transferring the FeS–Fe0 yield.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Kaur et al. (2024) directly support H2-driven oxaloacetate reductive amination over supported Ni. The balanced net reaction is sound, and rxn_014 correctly recognizes competing malate production. The principal uncertainty is operational: supported catalyst structure, H2 pressure and nitrogen concentration are unspecified. Neither the substrate-panel combined yields nor the low-ammonia alanine result establishes an Asp-specific yield here.
suggestions: Document the Ni support, loading and active surface, alongside the reference conditions of 22 °C, pH 8, 5 bar H2 and 72 hours.
Report Asp-specific selectivity against malate and pyruvate, and justify any environmental catalyst or pressure substitution experimentally.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Kaur et al. (2024) provide direct evidence that ground Fe–Ni meteorites catalyze this chemistry, supporting both the transformation and a naturally occurring catalyst class. The remaining gap concerns the actual compartment: exposed metallic surface area, corrosion state, H2 availability and reaction conditions are not specified. Meteorite powder results do not establish equivalent rates for intact or weathered material.
suggestions: Specify Fe–Ni composition, particle size, loading and a physically plausible source of reactive exposed surfaces.
Define H2 pressure, pH, ammonium concentration and residence time, and measure Asp production relative to competing oxaloacetate reactions.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Pd-mediated reductive amination is strongly supported by Kaur et al. (2024). The environmental uncertainty concerns catalyst implementation, not an intrinsic objection to Pd chemistry: the supporting experiments used Pd/C, whereas this reaction specifies only palladium. The broader substrate-panel yields and approximately 5% Asp in a more complex network are distinct experimental results and should not be conflated.
suggestions: Specify Pd oxidation state, support, dispersion and loading, with evidence that the proposed compartment contains a comparably active material.
Attach reaction-specific H2 pressure, temperature, pH and Asp yield data rather than combined amino-plus-hydroxy-acid yields.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Muchowska et al. (2019) support hydroxylamine/Fe0 conversion of ketoacids to amino acids, including Asp. The deterministic check establishes conservation with two Fe atoms, three protons and two product waters; this is not an unbalanced reaction. Separate compartments avoid the cited incompatibility with upstream Fe2+-driven chemistry. Nevertheless, the supplied evidence does not establish this transformation under an unspecified cool-pool regime.
suggestions: Encode the explicit stoichiometry: mol_007 + mol_008 + 2 mol_004 + 3 mol_005 -> mol_017 + 2 mol_006 + 2 mol_001.
Provide the actual amination-stage temperature, pH, concentrations and time from the supporting experiment, or validate the proposed cooler conditions.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Harrison et al. (2023) directly support Cu2+-promoted pyridoxamine transamination, with approximately 5% Asp within one hour. The equation correctly consumes pyridoxamine and produces pyridoxal; cofactor regeneration is unnecessary for the declared supplied-inventory boundary. The reaction is credible, but the network should identify which demonstrated temperature and pH conditions support its proposed compartment.
suggestions: Add a reaction-level citation and specify temperature, pH, Cu loading, donor concentration and reaction time.
Document Cu speciation and compare Asp formation with oxaloacetate decay under the selected conditions.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The supplied Harrison et al. (2023) findings report measurable Ni2+-promoted Asp formation, so this is not merely an unsupported catalyst substitution. However, the cited metal screen used 70 °C, and its results do not automatically establish useful conversion in an unspecified cool compartment. The lower confidence reflects this condition-specific evidence gap, not low yield alone.
suggestions: Supply Ni-specific Asp measurements and the corresponding temperature, pH, loading and duration.
Validate operation at the proposed compartment temperature rather than transferring Cu-specific yields or operating ranges.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Harrison et al. (2023) support measurable Al-promoted transamination under screening conditions. The net chemistry is balanced and plausible, but the proposed implementation is insufficiently established: the representative screen was at 70 °C, and nominal Al3+ addition does not establish the concentration or identity of active dissolved Al species near neutral pH. Separation from phosphate chemistry avoids one reported incompatibility but does not resolve hydrolysis and precipitation.
suggestions: Specify Al source, ligand environment, dissolved concentration, pH and temperature, accounting for hydrolysis and precipitation.
Demonstrate Al-specific Asp formation and competition with oxaloacetate decay under the proposed operating conditions.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Springsteen et al. (2018) strongly support the identified alpha-hydroxyglycine and beta-carboxyaspartate intermediates and the final Asp-forming decarboxylation. All three equations conserve atoms and charge. However, the reported 50% yield covers the malonate coupling/decarboxylation sequence using prepared alpha-hydroxyglycine, not a demonstrated unpurified three-step environmental sequence. Cold adduct preparation, prolonged concentrated coupling and Mg-assisted warming require explicit staging.
suggestions: Specify the reference sequence: concentrated ammonium medium near 0 °C; approximately 0.48 M malonate and 1 M bicarbonate at 23 °C for five days; then Mg addition and 60 °C for five hours.
Test carryover of the unpurified adduct-forming mixture into coupling and decarboxylation, and describe the thermal schedule and Mg inventory without assuming selective cleanup.

evaluation.network_feedback: This is a strong literature-grounded precursor-to-aspartate network, but it is not approved at the network threshold of 0.90. Structural validity is high: all 18 molecule nodes and 14 reaction nodes participate in a connected chemical-identity graph, IDs are consistent, and the authoritative balance check reports no conservation violations. rxn_006 requires only the stated small integer coefficients. The neutral precursor-pool and buffer-proton conventions are acceptable, and mol_017 represents the requested stereochemically unspecified aspartate. Catalyst-specific alternatives with identical net equations are legitimate operational pathways; their number is neither a strength nor a defect. The declared supplied-precursor boundary is respected: upstream CO2 fixation, continuous feedstock generation, pyridoxamine regeneration and physical pooling of separate compartments are not requirements for this assessment. Literature alignment is strong for the terminal transformations, although the reaction records lack their own citations and numerical operating conditions. The principal network-wide limitation is environmental specification: 'Biochemical' and 'cool aqueous' do not establish catalyst state, concentration, pH, pressure or residence time, and several supporting experiments involve warmer or staged conditions. rxn_013 and rxn_014 are chemically valid competing sinks and appropriately acknowledge oxaloacetate loss, but their inclusion alone does not establish favorable Asp-producing flux. Direct Asp formation is well supported; quantitative environmental productivity and accumulation remain unestablished and are appropriately not claimed. Problematic-reaction flags identify operational, environmental or documentation gaps, not atom/charge violations. Pathway approval uses the requested 0.80 threshold and is distinct from network approval.
